evidence.claim: Follow the Snake River canyon where springs emerge from rock
evidence.quote: The byway takes its name from the numerous streams and rivulets springing forth out of the east wall of that canyon

evidence.claim: US 30 drops into the Hagerman Valley and a canyon of the Snake River, where springs emerge from the east wall.
evidence.quote: The Thousand Springs Scenic Byway is a picturesque section of US 30 in southern Idaho between the towns of Bliss and Buhl, dipping down into the Hagerman Valley and a canyon of the Snake River.

evidence.claim: where springs emerge from the east wall
evidence.quote: numerous streams and rivulets springing forth out of the east wall of that canyon

evidence.claim: Many are visible from the road, with the river in front.
evidence.quote: many of them plainly visible from the road, with the panoramic river in the foreground.

evidence.claim: Visit Idaho presents Thousand Springs as one of the state’s scenic byways for its geological features, canyon views and waterfalls.
evidence.quote: Thousand Springs Scenic Byway gives road trippers a glimpse of some of Idaho’s remarkable geological wonders.

evidence.claim: canyon views and waterfalls
evidence.quote: this route features canyon views, quaint small towns and Thousand Springs State Park—an expansive park made up of six separate park units with stunning waterfalls

evidence.claim: Its itinerary covers 65.4 miles, with a listed driving time of one hour and 32 minutes.
evidence.quote: Length 65.4 miles 105.2 km Time 1 hour, 32 minutes

evidence.claim: US 30 was established in 1926 as part of the United States Numbered Highway System.
evidence.quote: US 30 was established in 1926 during the creation of the United States Numbered Highway System

evidence.claim: Across southern Idaho it followed Route 2 from the Oregon line to Burley.
evidence.quote: The highway crossed southern Idaho by following Route 2 between the Oregon state line and Burley

evidence.claim: Construction of the parallel freeway, then called I-80N and now I-84, began in the 1960s.
evidence.quote: Construction of I-80N (now I-84), a freeway that would parallel US 30 between Portland, Oregon, and northern Utah, began in the 1960s

evidence.claim: Sections of US 30 shifted onto the freeway as it opened, but at Bliss the numbered route leaves the interstate for the byway.
evidence.quote: Various sections of US 30 were relocated onto the new freeway as sections opened over the following two decades.

evidence.claim: at Bliss the numbered route leaves the interstate for the byway
evidence.quote: Then, in Bliss, US 30 leaves the freeway and enters the Thousand Springs Scenic Byway.

evidence.claim: An earlier crossing survives south of Hagerman: Owsley Bridge, built in 1920–21, carried a former alignment of US 30 across the Snake.
evidence.quote: Owsley Bridge is a historic bridge spanning the Snake River

evidence.claim: south of Hagerman
evidence.quote: south Hagerman

evidence.claim: Owsley Bridge, built in 1920–21, carried a former alignment of US 30
evidence.quote: was on the former routing of US‑30. It is a cantilevered Warren truss bridge built in 1920–21.

evidence.claim: From Bliss, travel southeast through Hagerman, Buhl and Filer to Twin Falls.
evidence.quote: Then, in Bliss, US 30 leaves the freeway and enters the Thousand Springs Scenic Byway. As US 30 approaches I-84, the route turns south and east, serving Hagerman, Buhl, Filer, and Twin Falls.

evidence.claim: The springs along the canyon are outlets of the Snake River Aquifer, which moves through porous volcanic rock.
evidence.quote: These springs are outlets from the Snake River Aquifer, which flows through thousands of square miles of porous volcanic rock

evidence.claim: Beyond Twin Falls, the tourism itinerary continues to Idaho 50 and turns north to I-84, with US 93 providing another northbound connection.
evidence.quote: Begins at I-84 near Bliss and follows U.S. 30 southeast through Twin Falls to Idaho 50, and then north on Idaho 50 to I-84. Also U.S. 93 from Twin Falls north to I-84.

evidence.claim: Springs emerge from the canyon’s east wall, with many visible beyond the river from the road.
evidence.quote: numerous streams and rivulets springing forth out of the east wall of that canyon, many of them plainly visible from the road, with the panoramic river in the foreground.

evidence.claim: Thousand Springs State Park joins several landscapes under one name.
evidence.quote: Thousand Springs State Park is a public recreation and nature preservation area consisting of multiple units

evidence.claim: It was created in 2005 by merging four existing state parks in the Hagerman Valley, with another unit added later.
evidence.quote: The state park was created in 2005, when four existing state parks in the Hagerman Valley were merged into a single entity, with an additional unit subsequently added to the complex.

evidence.claim: At Malad Gorge, the Malad River has cut a canyon 250 feet deep below a 60-foot waterfall.
evidence.quote: Malad Gorge is a 250-foot-deep (76 m) canyon formed by the Malad River, downstream from a 60-foot (18 m) waterfall.

evidence.claim: Elsewhere in the park, Box Canyon has walls 250 feet high and a 20-foot waterfall.
evidence.quote: This 350-acre (140 ha) box canyon has 250-foot-high (76 m) walls.

evidence.claim: Box Canyon has walls 250 feet high and a 20-foot waterfall
evidence.quote: There is a 20-foot (6.1 m) waterfall.

evidence.claim: The Nature Conservancy bought the Box Canyon property in 1999 and completed its transfer to the state in 2016.
evidence.quote: The 350-acre (140 ha) property was developed by the Nature Conservancy which purchased the site in 1999, then completed its transfer to the state in 2016.

evidence.claim: Ritter Island, another unit, lies between two large springs along the Snake River.
evidence.quote: This unit lies along the Snake River between two large springs.

evidence.claim: Hagerman’s fossil record includes horses, camels and river otters.
evidence.quote:
Hagerman horse, Equus simplicidens, formerly known as Plesippus shoshonensis
Camelops, an extinct genus of camel that once inhabited North America
Lontra weiri, oldest New World River otter

evidence.claim: The deposits preserve a Pliocene landscape, with fossils dating from 3.07 million to at least four million years ago.
evidence.quote: These fossils date from 3.07 million to at least 4 million years ago in age

evidence.claim: The Hagerman Horse Quarry has yielded 20 complete skeletons as well as partial skeletons of Equus simplicidens.
evidence.quote: The Hagerman Horse Quarry fossil beds have produced 20 complete skeletons and a number of partial skeletons of this zebra-like ancestor of today's horse.

evidence.claim: The beds became a National Natural Landmark in 1975 and a national monument in 1988.
evidence.quote: The fossil beds, including the historic Smithsonian Horse Quarry, were designated a National Natural Landmark in 1975 and was reclassified as a National Monument in 1988.

evidence.claim: In 2016, researchers began a project to date individual fossil sites more closely and reconstruct the ancient landscapes they represent.
evidence.quote: In 2016, the Hagerman Paleontology, Environments, and Tephrochronology (PET) Project began their investigations into the geologic history at Hagerman with a focus on better dating individual fossil localities on the Monument and reconstructing the ancient landscapes that were there during the Pliocene.

evidence.claim: The assemblage also includes birds, fish, amphibians and turtles, extending the record beyond large mammals.
evidence.quote: A rich assemblage of other mammals, as well as birds, fish, amphibians, turtles, and invertebrates

evidence.claim: Buhl’s name points to the financing behind the Magic Valley’s irrigation.
evidence.quote: It is named for Frank H. Buhl of Sharon, Pennsylvania, a major investor in a Carey Act project known as the Twin Falls South Side Project

evidence.claim: Founded in 1906, the town was named for Frank H. Buhl, a Pennsylvania investor in the Twin Falls South Side Project.
evidence.quote: Buhl was founded on April 17, 1906. It is named for Frank H. Buhl of Sharon, Pennsylvania

evidence.claim: That project introduced large-scale irrigation to the valley in the early twentieth century.
evidence.quote: which introduced large-scale irrigation to the Magic Valley in the early 20th century.

evidence.claim: US 30 passes through town, and numerous trout hatcheries operate in the surrounding area.
evidence.quote: Buhl is the location of numerous hatcheries in the immediate surrounding area

evidence.claim: US 30 passes through town
evidence.quote: U.S. Route 30 passes through Buhl

flags: Visit Idaho describes a 65.4-mile itinerary through Twin Falls to Idaho 50, plus a US 93 connection. The highway article also describes the narrower Bliss–Buhl section as the byway. Used tourism for full route scope; no designation date is cached.

Current Buhl claim “by its own account” has no named local source in the cache. Removed that attribution, the nickname and the undated national production-share assertion; kept the supported hatchery presence. Buhl is shorter because evidence beyond basic history is thin.
Park unit counts differ: tourism and the monument article say six; the park article names five. Omitted a current count.

Preserved the state-park coordinate and title, but changed kind to separate excursion because this is a multi-unit park. It is ordered by its northern Malad Gorge anchor; Box Canyon is another unit, not that map pin.
Hagerman species totals differ between the city and monument articles. Omitted totals and the simplified ancestor claim; no fossil-quarry access is asserted.
Material puts Twin Falls at mile 1.07 despite the other strip miles and cached route order. Followed the cached Bliss–Hagerman–Buhl–Filer–Twin Falls sequence.
